title: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh
hook: the Ansar chief whose death shook the Throne (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Ayyub, who moved downstairs so his guest could sleep above. Your line was: the host. What did you notice about a guest today? Day eight hundred fifty-six.

The Throne of the Most Merciful shook. That's the sentence. Jabir ibn Abdullah says he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say it, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it, in a chapter about one man. Not a prophet. Not a king. The chief of a clan in Medina, wounded in battle, who died of the wound. What kind of life gets a sentence like that at its end? Today: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh.
screen: `THE THRONE SHOOK.` → `NOT A PROPHET, NOT A KING.` → `WHAT KIND OF LIFE?`

segments.voice: Sa'd was a leader of the Aws, a tribe of Medina, and the early biographies say that when he accepted Islam, his clan followed him. So he wasn't a private believer. He was a chief, with people looking at him. Bukhari shows what that looked like. Sa'd went to Mecca to perform the umrah, the lesser pilgrimage, staying with an old friend there. Abu Jahl, a leader of the Prophet's opponents, stopped him at the Kaaba and sneered that he was walking around safely after giving shelter to the Prophet's people. Sa'd didn't lower his voice. If you stop me from this, he said, I'll stop you from something worse: your trade road to Syria, which runs past Medina. A chief speaking as a chief, for the people under his protection. At the battle of the Trench, Sa'd was hit by an arrow in the arm. We met the tent where he was cared for, Rufaydah's tent in the mosque, on an earlier day. In his last days he was also asked to give a judgment in a hard and painful case, one the histories record and readers still wrestle with; that story needs its own day. The wound did not heal, and he died of it. That's when the Prophet said the Throne shook. And Bukhari adds another scene. Someone gave the Prophet a garment of silk, and people kept touching it, amazed at how soft it was. The Prophet said: the handkerchiefs of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Paradise are better than this. A handkerchief, a small, everyday thing, and still finer than the softest thing in the room. Sa'd held one role, chief of his people, and he held it the same way in Mecca, in battle, and in a tent with a wound that wouldn't close. The throne shook.
screen: `A CHIEF, WITH PEOPLE WATCHING.` · `FACING ABU JAHL AT THE KAABA.` · `AN ARROW AT THE TRENCH.` · `HANDKERCHIEFS FINER THAN SILK.` · then, large: `THE THRONE SHOOK.`

segments.voice: The practice: be sincere in one role. Settle, and breathe. You hold more than one role. Parent, child, friend, worker, neighbor, member of something. Let them pass by, one by one. Then choose one. Breathe in, and ask: in this role, where am I one person in public and another in private? Breathe out, and let one small difference close. Not all of them. One. If you pray, you can ask for sincerity, which Muslims call ikhlas, in that one role. The bell holds the time.
Sa'd. The chief of Medina who stood up to Abu Jahl, was wounded at the Trench, and at whose death, the Prophet said, the Throne shook. Today's word.
Your line: the throne shook. Today, in the one role you chose, act the same way whether anyone is watching or not. Day eight hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Sa'd ibn Mu'adh from reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, above all the Prophet's words that the Throne of the Most Merciful shook at his death.

fork.setup: you are Sa'd, at the Kaaba in Mecca. Abu Jahl sneers that you walk safely after sheltering the Prophet's people. what do you do?
options: answer: stop me, and I'll stop your trade road to Syria.
fork.reveal: Bukhari keeps his answer: block me from this, and I'll block something worse for you, your road to Syria.

original.note: Arabic: the Throne shook, the words the Prophet said at Sa'd's death.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chief who died in battle.
what it means: a leader who held his role the same way in Mecca, at war, and wounded, and whose death the Prophet marked with the Throne shaking.
what a scholar hears: Bukhari has the Throne of the Most Merciful shaking at his death, and the handkerchiefs finer than silk, in the chapter on his virtues.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3803 (the Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3802 (the handkerchiefs of Sa'd in Paradise are better than this silk)
Sahih al-Bukhari 3950 (Sa'd and Abu Jahl at the Kaaba; the trade road to Syria)
Sahih al-Bukhari 463 (Sa'd wounded at the Trench; the tent in the mosque)
Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah, via Ibn Hisham (his clan follows him into Islam)

notes: Hadith numbers (Bukhari 3802, 3803, 3950, 463) cited from memory; confirm.
He is described only as having come to Islam in Medina; no years given.
Aws described simply as 'a tribe of Medina'.
His clan following him into Islam is from the sira, attributed to 'the early biographies'; confirm.
Sa'd's judgment concerning the Banu Qurayzah is mentioned only in one sentence ('a hard and painful case... that story needs its own day'). Keeper should decide how, and whether, the path treats it.
Bukhari 3803 includes a dispute over whether 'the Throne' or 'the bier' shook; the script follows the Throne wording in the index.
Original: confirm vowels and stress of ihtazza al-'arsh.
Editor: fixed 'pilgrimage' to umrah per Bukhari 3950; cut the doubled 'in Medina' in the hook; replaced 'the least of what he'd have' (not in Bukhari 3802) with a plainer line.
